---
title: "Estimating EIR from prevalence"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("styles/mint.mplstyle")
```

A parasite survey gives a prevalence, and the transmission model needs an EIR. `estimint`
inverts the one into the other and returns the EIR that would have sustained the measured
prevalence. Prevalence alone is not enough. Six covariates describing the setting go in
alongside it.

## The prevalence model

Load the model by name. It ships inside the wheel, so the call is offline and takes
milliseconds.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from estimint import load_xgb_model, run_xgb_model

prev_model = load_xgb_model("prevalence")
prev_model["features"]
```

All seven columns are required. Six describe the setting, and the seventh, `prev_y9`, carries
the driving input.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dn0_use` | Probability a mosquito dies on contact with a net. From `calculate_dn0`. |
| `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1 |
| `phi_bednets` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed |
| `seasonal` | 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal |
| `itn_use` | ITN coverage, 0 to 1. From `calculate_dn0`. |
| `irs_use` | IRS coverage, 0 to 1 |
| `prev_y9` | Parasite prevalence in the deployment year, 0 to 1 |

A missing column raises a `ValueError` naming it. `prevalence` is accepted as an alias for
`prev_y9` and copied across, which is convenient, because `estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta`
expects that name too. `run_xgb_model` takes the frame and the model and returns a plain NumPy
array, one element per row.

```{python}
setting = dict(
    dn0_use=0.33, Q0=0.87, phi_bednets=0.82,
    seasonal=0.0, itn_use=0.6, irs_use=0.0,
)

one = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": 0.30}])
eir = run_xgb_model(one, prev_model)

type(eir), eir
```

A prevalence of 30% in this setting implies about 13.4 infectious bites per person per year.

## Sweeping prevalence

Sweeping the prevalence with the setting held fixed shows that the EIR is nowhere near linear
in it, and that doubling prevalence from 0.30 to 0.60 raises the EIR roughly fivefold rather
than doubling it. Between 0.60 and 0.75 it more than doubles again.

```{python}
sweep = pd.DataFrame(
    [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75]]
)
sweep["eir"] = run_xgb_model(sweep, prev_model)

sweep[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(2)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Inferred EIR against prevalence, holding the setting fixed."
#| fig-alt: "A teal line rising slowly from near zero at 5% prevalence then climbing very steeply above 60% prevalence, reaching about 160 infectious bites per person per year at 75%."
import numpy as np

grid = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in np.linspace(0.05, 0.75, 71)])
grid["eir"] = run_xgb_model(grid, prev_model)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(grid["prevalence"], grid["eir"], color="#00d4aa")
ax.set_xlabel("Prevalence")
ax.set_ylabel("EIR (infectious bites per person per year)")
plt.show()
```

The teal curve is nearly flat below a prevalence of 0.3 and climbs almost vertically above 0.6.
This is because prevalence saturates while transmission does not, so once most of the
population already carries parasites, a further rise in prevalence can only come from a very
large rise in the bites behind it. An input a few points out at 70% therefore moves the
inferred EIR by tens of bites per year, while the same error at 20% moves it by less than one.

## The role of the setting

The same measured prevalence implies different EIRs in different settings, and net coverage is
the covariate that moves the answer most. The district in the running example has a prevalence
of 0.45, pyrethroid resistance of 0.30, and pyrethroid-only nets. Only the coverage varies
below.

```{python}
from estimint import calculate_dn0

rows = []
for coverage in [0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]:
    nets = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=coverage)
    rows.append({
        "coverage": coverage,
        "dn0_use": nets.dn0,
        "itn_use": nets.itn_use,
        "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0.0, "irs_use": 0.0,
        "prevalence": 0.45,
    })

nets_vs_eir = pd.DataFrame(rows)
nets_vs_eir["eir"] = run_xgb_model(nets_vs_eir, prev_model)

nets_vs_eir[["coverage", "dn0_use", "itn_use", "prevalence", "eir"]].round(3)
```

Every row reports the same prevalence, and the inferred EIR still rises by roughly two thirds
down the column. This is because a district that holds 45% prevalence under 90% net coverage
must be absorbing far more infectious bites than one that holds the same prevalence with no
nets at all. The nets have already suppressed a large share of them. Understating `itn_use`,
the error described in [Nets and dn0](nets-and-dn0.qmd), therefore biases the EIR downwards.

## The global model

`set_global_model` registers a model as the default, after which `run_xgb_model` may be called
with the frame alone, and `get_global_model` returns whatever is currently registered.

```{python}
from estimint import set_global_model, get_global_model

set_global_model(prev_model)
run_xgb_model(one)
```

```{python}
get_global_model()["class"]
```

Note that the global slot holds exactly one model. Pass it explicitly in any script that
touches more than one of the three, because a stray `set_global_model` elsewhere changes what
an unqualified call resolves to.

::: {.callout-note}
## The valid range

`prev_y9` is clamped to `[0.005, 0.80]`, and values outside that band are quietly pulled to the
nearest edge. No warning is raised.

```{python}
edges = pd.DataFrame(
    [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.001, 0.005, 0.80, 0.95]]
)
edges["eir"] = run_xgb_model(edges, prev_model)

edges[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(3)
```

Note that a prevalence of 0.001 and one of 0.005 return the same EIR, as do 0.80 and 0.95, and
that a sweep producing an implausibly flat EIR at either end has almost always hit this clamp.
The epidemiology is rarely the cause.
:::

The same inversion runs from entomological data where there is no parasite survey, and

[Mosquito density and EIR](mosquito-density.qmd) for the EIR when the vector population changes.
